title: Come and see
hookLine: a song of praise that stops to say: don't take my word for it
carry: ehipassiko: the dhamma asks to be tested
tomorrow: what does Ông chant before he drives home in the dark?

lines: A VERSE OF PRAISE FOR THE DHAMMA.
cards: A restaurant with a sign in the window that says don't trust our reviews, come taste it, would get your attention. Praise usually asks to be believed: five stars, best in town, life-changing.
Buddhist chanting books have a verse of praise for the dhamma, the teaching, and right in the middle of it sits an odd word: ehipassiko. Come and see.
A song meant to honor something stops halfway to say, in effect, don't take my word for it. So why would anyone put that in a hymn?

teach.h: A VERSE THAT PRAISES THE DHAMMA.
teach.b: Here's the verse, as it's chanted. Svakkhato bhagavata dhammo: well taught by the Blessed One is the dhamma. Then its qualities, one after another.
Sanditthiko: visible here and now, in this life. Akaliko: not a matter of time, nothing you wait ages for.
Ehipassiko: from ehi, come, and passa, see. Of the come-and-see kind. Opanayiko: leading onward.

teach.h: KNOWN BY THE WISE, EACH FOR THEMSELVES.
teach.b: And the last line: paccattam veditabbo vinnuhi, to be known by the wise, each for themselves. So the puzzle has its answer. The praise is the invitation.
What the verse honors about the teaching is that it can be checked, here and now, in a life. But look at that last word, vinnuhi: by the wise.

teach.h: NOT ANYTHING GOES: WHAT DOES IT DO?
teach.b: Come and see doesn't mean anything goes. In the talk to the Kalamas, villagers tired of rival teachers, the Buddha lists things not to lean on alone: reports, tradition, scripture, even clever reasoning.
The test he offers is what a teaching does when it's lived. Does it lead to harm and suffering, or to welfare and happiness? And would the wise blame it or praise it?
So come and see, and look closely, in good company.

how: In Theravada temples the verse on the qualities of the dhamma is chanted in Pali after the verse on the Buddha's qualities and before the one on the sangha, often in morning and evening chanting.

o: a promise that awakening comes quickly to all
a welcome to visitors walking into a temple hall
an invitation to check the teaching for yourself

games.q: the dhamma's qualities — tap the pairs.
p: known by the wise, each for themselves

s: the Buddha said: believe nothing unless it agrees with your own reason
a popular paraphrase, not the text. the Kalama talk even lists clever reasoning among things not to lean on alone.
ehipassiko is built from ehi, come, and passa, see
come and see: a teaching of the kind you can check for yourself.
come and see means each person decides what's true, no help needed
the verse says known by the wise, each for themselves, and the Kalama test asks what the wise would blame or praise.

games.q: a new app promises your anxiety gone in seven days, guaranteed, and the reviews glow. by the dhamma verse's own test, what's your move?
o: trust it: that many good reviews can't be wrong.
try it, watch honestly what it does in your life, and ask someone wise.
skip it: anything that promises results must be a scam.
games.why: come and see: check a teaching by what it does when lived, here and now, and bring the wise into it. not blind trust, not blanket rejection.

practice: Chant the dhamma verse once, slowly, from the screen. Then write ehipassiko on any scrap of paper, and under it one teaching from these weeks you'd like to test, maybe hatred never ends by hatred.
For the rest of the sit, hold it up against one real memory of your own, and just look at what happened.

wordCard.voice: Come and see: ehipassiko, from ehi, come, and passa, see. A teaching praised because you can check it yourself.

orig.note: Pali, in Devanagari letters: ehi, come, and passa, see; 'of the come-and-see kind'.

carryVoice: Hold on to this: ehipassiko, the dhamma asks to be tested. Come and see, then look closely, in good company. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: SN 11.3 (Dhajagga Sutta): the qualities of the dhamma, svakkhato bhagavata dhammo … paccattam veditabbo vinnuhi
AN 3.65 (Kalama Sutta): not by reports, tradition, scripture or reasoning alone; what leads to harm or welfare, blamed or praised by the wise
